paragraphs: Predicting one token at a time can seem disconnected from evaluating where an entire sequence is going. This paper connects autoregressive models with energy-based models, which also naturally describe optimal policies in post-training alignment. Its aim is to explain how these two perspectives can represent the same underlying functions.

Starting from the probability chain rule, the authors establish a one-to-one correspondence between autoregressive and energy-based models in function space. They show that this correspondence is a special case of the soft Bellman equation from maximum entropy reinforcement learning. This provides a mathematical connection between sequential token probabilities and a formulation associated with planning.

Using that connection, the paper derives an equivalence between supervised learning in the two model classes and gives theoretical error bounds for distilling energy-based models into autoregressive ones. These results clarify how next-token prediction can accommodate lookahead. They concern a relationship between model functions and learning objectives, rather than an empirical claim that every language model reliably plans.
icml-2026-autoregressive-language-models.tldr: A mathematical correspondence between autoregressive and energy-based models explains how next-token prediction can support lookahead.

paragraphs: Mixed-integer programming methods can generate many related linear programs while deciding which branches to explore or tightening variable bounds. This paper asks how to solve those related problems together on GPUs. The opportunity lies in organizing the work as a batch, so the hardware can process multiple optimization problems in parallel.

The authors extend the primal-dual hybrid gradient algorithm, a first-order optimization method, to handle these batches. The central computational change replaces repeated matrix-vector operations with matrix-matrix operations. That change matters because the batched formulation makes better use of GPU architectures, producing significant computational advantages for the workloads examined.

Case studies identify problem sizes where the first-order approach outperforms traditional simplex-based solvers, with the crossover depending on the computing environment. The result therefore supports selective use of GPUs within integer programming. The authors argue that some operations could be performed fully on GPUs where CPU implementations instead use lightweight heuristics, changing which computations are practical inside a larger solver.
icml-2026-batched-first-order-methods-fo.tldr: Batching related linear programs lets a first-order solver exploit GPUs and outperform simplex methods in identified computational settings.

paragraphs: Counting fruit becomes difficult when individual objects are tiny, overlap heavily, and blend into surrounding leaves. The paper introduces DIOCblueberry to study this extreme setting. Relative to FSC147, its images contain 1.9 times as many instances on average, averaging 108, while the average bounding-box pixel ratio is 7.9 times smaller.

The proposed MaskCount system tackles these problems through a coarse-to-fine process with semantic guidance. It uses CLIP to produce approximate segmentation masks that suppress background regions. A contrastive training objective makes fruit and foliage features easier to distinguish, while an edge-aware cropping mechanism addresses objects cut off at crop boundaries in dense clusters.

Experiments report new state-of-the-art performance on DIOCblueberry, reducing mean absolute error by 49.16% and root mean squared error by 70.50%, alongside strong generalization to other agricultural scenes. The contribution combines a benchmark that exposes severe visual ambiguity with a method designed around that ambiguity. Its components address background confusion, small object scale, and boundary truncation within the same counting framework.
icml-2026-benchmarking-dense-and-indisce.tldr: DIOCblueberry tests counting under extreme crowding and camouflage, while MaskCount substantially reduces counting errors on the benchmark.

paragraphs: Sampling from an unnormalized density means generating examples when the target is specified without its overall normalization constant. Diffusion-based approaches can tackle this problem, and matching objectives have made them more scalable. However, existing approaches can require restrictive starting distributions or optimization procedures that are unstable, creating trade-offs in practical use.

The paper interprets these matching methods as particular fixed-point iterations based on Nelson’s relation. From this shared formulation, the authors develop a single objective for learning stochastic transport between arbitrary prior and target distributions. The intended benefit is to combine flexibility in the starting distribution with scalable and stable training.

A damped version of the iteration adds regularization to mitigate mode collapse, where sampling loses diversity across distinct parts of the target distribution. Experiments report sampling at unprecedented scales while retaining mode diversity, with state-of-the-art results on complex synthetic densities and high-dimensional molecular benchmarks. These findings support the proposed formulation as a way to expand sampling scale without sacrificing the diversity observed in those evaluations.
icml-2026-bridge-matching-sampler-scalab.tldr: Bridge Matching Sampler learns flexible diffusion transports with a stable objective and regularization that helps preserve sampling diversity.

paragraphs: Causal discovery can leave uncertainty about whether two variables are connected and which direction the connection takes. This paper proposes using expert judgments to refine that uncertainty through targeted questions. Its Bayesian framework maintains a distribution over possible directed acyclic graphs, allowing multiple causal explanations to remain under consideration.

The method starts from any black-box posterior obtained from observational data. It models noisy expert answers with a three-way likelihood covering local edge existence and direction, then updates a flexible particle approximation of the graph posterior. Questions are selected using expected information gain: the method favors queries whose possible categorical answers are expected to reduce uncertainty efficiently.

Experiments on synthetic graphs, protein signaling data, and a human gene perturbation benchmark show faster posterior concentration and better recovery of directed effects under tight query budgets. The practical contribution is a way to spend limited expert attention on informative local relationships. Accounting for noisy judgments also lets those answers influence the posterior without treating every expert response as an unquestionable fact.
icml-2026-causal-preference-elicitation-.tldr: Targeted questions about causal edges help a Bayesian discovery system learn more from limited, potentially noisy expert input.

paragraphs: Meta-reinforcement learning trains across environments so a policy can adapt to a new setting with few training steps. Many approaches assume that unobserved confounders can be ruled out beforehand. This paper studies the harder situation where observational data from multiple heterogeneous environments are confounded, complicating what the learner can infer about decisions and outcomes.

The authors introduce an augmentation procedure that can be added to standard meta-learning algorithms such as MAML. It uses partial identification to construct candidate environments consistent with the observations, then generates posterior counterfactual trajectories from them. These trajectories represent alternative sequences compatible with what is known, providing additional material for learning a policy initialization.

The initialization is chosen to support generalization in the target domain. Within the paper’s causal meta-learning formulation, the theoretical analysis guarantees a solution that minimizes generalization loss on future inference tasks. The approach matters because it incorporates uncertainty about the environments behind confounded observations into meta-training, rather than requiring the training data to exclude hidden confounding from the outset.
icml-2026-counterfactual-bootstrap-for-r.tldr: Counterfactual trajectory augmentation enables causal meta-reinforcement learning from confounded observations across heterogeneous environments.

paragraphs: Multimodal dataset distillation compresses a large collection into a small set of synthetic pairs, such as images paired with text. Existing methods match teacher and student training trajectories within each modality. Keeping model checkpoints and repeatedly optimizing inside another optimization loop makes this process expensive in both storage and computation.

Analytic parameter matching replaces that inner optimization with analytically derived parameters for modality projectors. It then matches the teacher’s and student’s derived projector parameters. The method needs only two cached matrices in place of checkpoint-heavy storage and computes the analytic parameters in one forward pass, directly addressing both sources of overhead.

Experiments report up to 65 times lower storage requirements and 9.6 times faster distillation, with scaling to 1,000 synthetic pairs. Image-text and audio-text evaluations demonstrate useful cross-modal retrieval, including reported Flickr30k scores of 12.8 IR@1 and 17.8 TR@1 with 100 pairs. Additional evaluations show generalization across architectures and in zero-shot classification, suggesting that the compressed data retain usefulness beyond a single model configuration.
icml-2026-efficient-multi-modal-dataset-.tldr: Analytic parameter matching makes multimodal dataset distillation cheaper by replacing checkpoint trajectories and inner optimization with directly computed projector parameters.

paragraphs: Human vision concentrates detail near the center of gaze while preserving a wider, lower-resolution view of the surroundings. Most computer vision systems instead process images at uniform resolution, making large, detailed views computationally demanding. FOVI explores a biologically inspired interface that gives models access to unevenly distributed visual detail.

The interface maps a retina-like sensor arrangement with variable resolution onto a uniformly dense sensor manifold inspired by primary visual cortex. Local receptive fields are defined through nearest neighbors on this manifold. A new kernel mapping technique then enables convolution over those neighborhoods, allowing the model to process the reformatted input.

The authors demonstrate both a complete nearest-neighbor convolutional architecture and an adaptation of the DINOv3 vision transformer using low-rank adaptation. These systems deliver competitive performance with only a fraction of the pixels and computation required by full-resolution, non-foveated baselines. The findings support foveated interfaces as a route toward efficient high-resolution egocentric sensing, where selected regions can receive detailed attention while the broader scene remains available as context.
icml-2026-fovi-a-biologically-inspired-f.tldr: FOVI gives vision models a retina-inspired input interface that achieves competitive performance using fewer pixels and less computation.

paragraphs: Identifying an unknown molecule from a tandem mass spectrum remains difficult at high throughput. FRIGID addresses this by generating molecular structures with a diffusion language model. The model conditions on spectra through intermediate molecular fingerprints and determined chemical formulae, while its training scales to hundreds of millions of unlabeled structures.

The framework also makes additional computation useful during inference. Forward fragmentation models identify fragments that are inconsistent with the observed spectrum. FRIGID then targets those portions for remasking and denoising, refining a proposed structure using feedback about spectral consistency. This gives the generation process a focused mechanism for revising problematic fragments.

The diffusion base already performs strongly, and the refinement procedure substantially improves accuracy. The paper reports more than 18% Top-1 accuracy on MassSpecGym and three times the Top-1 accuracy of leading methods on NPLIB1. Further experiments find log-linear performance scaling with inference compute. That observed relationship suggests a promising direction for continued improvement through additional refinement, while remaining an empirical finding from the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-frigid-scaling-diffusion-based.tldr: FRIGID combines large-scale molecular diffusion training with spectrum-guided refinement to improve structure identification as inference compute increases.

paragraphs: In the repeated game studied here, a leader commits to a strategy and a follower responds according to a private type. Each round draws that type independently from an unknown distribution. The leader also lacks knowledge of the possible follower payoffs, making the learning problem more demanding than settings where those payoffs are supplied.

The objective is to limit regret relative to repeatedly using an optimal commitment chosen with full knowledge of the game. The paper first shows that no-regret learning is impossible when the leader sees only the follower’s chosen best response. Observing actions alone therefore provides insufficient feedback for this objective in the unknown-type setting.

The authors then consider richer feedback that reveals the follower’s type after each round as well. Under this feedback model, they propose an algorithm with regret of approximately square-root order in the number of rounds, suppressing logarithmic factors and dependence on other parameters. The contrast identifies feedback about private types as a decisive ingredient separating an impossibility result from a positive learning guarantee.
icml-2026-learning-in-bayesian-stackelbe.tldr: With unknown follower payoffs, no-regret Stackelberg learning is impossible from action feedback alone but achievable with revealed types.

paragraphs: The paper treats in-context learning as an associative memory that updates while processing a sequence. In gated linear attention, that memory has limited capacity and can suffer interference on long sequences. Palimpsa reframes the problem as continual learning: the model must acquire new information while preserving accumulated knowledge that remains useful.

Its mechanism is Bayesian metaplasticity, which links how readily each attention state changes to a corresponding importance state. A prior distribution grounds that importance in accumulated knowledge. This makes the balance between remembering, learning, and forgetting part of the model’s memory update, directly addressing the stability-plasticity dilemma.

The authors derive several gated linear attention models through particular architectural choices and posterior approximations, and identify Mamba2 as a Palimpsa special case dominated by forgetting. They use this connection to transform non-metaplastic models into metaplastic versions with substantially greater memory capacity. Experiments show consistent improvements over baselines on Multi-Query Associative Recall and Commonsense Reasoning tasks, supporting the value of adapting memory plasticity to learned importance.
icml-2026-learning-to-remember-learn-and.tldr: Palimpsa improves attention-based memory by using Bayesian importance estimates to control what changes, persists, and is forgotten.

paragraphs: Imitation learning becomes especially challenging when only a small amount of expert behavior is available. In this setting, methods built around extensive pretraining or high-capacity architectures can be difficult to apply. Noise-Guided Transport focuses on extracting useful behavior from limited demonstrations with a lightweight learning method that avoids those requirements.

The method formulates imitation as an optimal transport problem and solves it through adversarial training. It is off-policy, includes uncertainty estimation in its design, and requires neither pretraining nor a specialized architecture. The authors also describe it as easy to implement and tune, emphasizing a combination of data efficiency and a relatively simple learning setup.

Despite that simplicity, experiments show strong performance on challenging continuous-control problems, including high-dimensional Humanoid tasks. The reported ultra-low-data settings include demonstrations containing as few as 20 transitions. These findings indicate that a transport-based adversarial formulation can be effective with extremely sparse expert data in the tested tasks, making it a useful approach to imitation when demonstrations are the central constraint.
icml-2026-noise-guided-transport-imitati.tldr: Noise-Guided Transport learns continuous-control behavior from very limited demonstrations using a lightweight adversarial transport formulation.

paragraphs: Rademacher complexity measures the size of a function class in a way that supports generalization bounds. A classical contraction result controls how this complexity changes when functions are composed with a fixed Lipschitz function. This paper asks whether analogous control remains available for sequential and offset complexities, which arise in online learning and squared-loss prediction.

The authors show that contraction does extend to these quantities when the function class satisfies additional structural assumptions. However, the bounds incur polylogarithmic factors. This gives a qualified positive result: composing functions can still be analyzed, but the classical relationship requires both extra conditions and a weaker quantitative bound.

The paper also proves that the logarithmic factors cannot generally be eliminated and that, without the structural assumptions, such contraction inequalities can fail altogether. These negative results establish a fundamental difference from classical Rademacher complexity. For analyses of composed function classes, they explain why online learning and squared-loss regression require particular care when translating complexity estimates into sample-complexity conclusions.
icml-2026-on-contraction-of-sequential-a.tldr: Sequential and offset Rademacher complexities admit contraction only with structural conditions and generally unavoidable logarithmic losses.

paragraphs: In a hidden-action contract problem, a principal offers payments tied to outcomes to motivate an agent whose costly action cannot be observed. The principal may also be uncertain about the agent and the environment. Repeated interaction provides a way to learn better payments from experience in settings such as crowdsourcing and task delegation.

Existing online approaches can achieve regret that grows sublinearly with the number of interactions, yet still depend exponentially on the size of the problem. This means favorable learning over time can coexist with poor scaling as the instance becomes larger. The paper focuses on removing that exponential dependence.

Its positive result assumes that the principal knows a set of possible agent actions while remaining uncertain about which are actually available. Under this knowledge assumption, the problematic exponential growth can be avoided. The contribution identifies a useful middle ground in the information available to the principal: knowing the candidate action set can make learning more tractable even when the agent’s actual capabilities remain unknown.
icml-2026-online-contract-design-with-un.tldr: Knowing a candidate set of agent actions can remove exponential problem-size dependence in online contract learning despite unknown action availability.

paragraphs: Matching scarce resources or positions involves deciding both which assignments are efficient and how assignments are distributed across groups. This paper defines group fairness within optimal transport by requiring the probability of matching members of each pair of groups to meet a prescribed target. Fairness is therefore expressed directly through the transport plan.

The authors first modify the Sinkhorn algorithm to efficiently compute plans satisfying these targets exactly. Because exact fairness can substantially worsen matching quality, they also develop two relaxations. One penalizes unfairness within the transport objective; the other uses bilevel optimization to learn a ground cost that induces a fair transport solution.

The penalized formulation comes with finite-sample complexity guarantees. For the learned-cost approach, the paper bounds how far fairness may deviate when matching previously unseen data. Empirical results illustrate the trade-off between fairness and transport cost. Together, these contributions provide ways to enforce prescribed group relationships exactly or explore relaxations when strict targets carry a substantial matching-quality cost.
icml-2026-optimal-transport-under-group-.tldr: The paper develops exact and relaxed optimal transport methods for meeting group matching targets while examining their cost to matching quality.

paragraphs: This paper proposes measuring privacy through a Bayesian game-theoretic framework. Its goal is to support privacy definitions tailored to particular purposes while providing rigorous justification for them. The same framework also offers a way to assess established privacy guarantees, connecting the design of new definitions with the interpretation of existing ones.

The authors show that pure and probabilistic differential privacy fit within their framework as special cases. They also derive new interpretations of the post-processing inequality in these settings. These connections matter because they anchor the broader framework in recognized privacy notions while allowing those notions to be understood from a common game-theoretic perspective.

The paper further establishes that privacy guarantees can be given for deterministic algorithms, a category overlooked by current privacy standards according to the abstract. This result expands the kinds of algorithms that the framework can assess. It does not say that every deterministic algorithm is private; the contribution is a framework capable of rigorously establishing such guarantees where its purpose-driven definitions support them.
icml-2026-persuasive-privacy-485f692eee.tldr: A Bayesian game-theoretic framework unifies established privacy notions and supports purpose-driven guarantees, including for deterministic algorithms.

paragraphs: Generative models based on differential equations move samples from a prior distribution toward a data distribution. Some applications also need to reverse that computation accurately. Standard numerical solvers accumulate discretization errors, so integrating backward does not exactly undo the forward calculation. Existing inversion approaches also face stability and convergence limitations and are restricted to ordinary differential equations.

Rex is a family of reversible exponential Runge-Kutta solvers covering both ordinary and stochastic differential equations. The construction uses Lawson methods to turn explicit Runge-Kutta schemes, including stochastic ones, into algebraically reversible schemes. This makes reversibility a property of the numerical method itself rather than relying on backward integration to cancel accumulated errors.

The theoretical analysis establishes arbitrary-order convergence and a nonzero region of linear stability. Experiments demonstrate reconstruction near machine precision, alongside improvements in Boltzmann sampling with flow models and image generation and editing with diffusion models. The combination matters for applications needing both accurate inversion and useful numerical behavior, with empirical reconstruction precision supporting the practical value of the reversible construction.
icml-2026-rex-a-family-of-reversible-exp.tldr: Rex converts explicit Runge-Kutta methods into reversible ODE and SDE solvers, achieving near-machine-precision reconstruction in experiments.

paragraphs: Trained attention weights exhibit recurring spectral patterns, including low-rank structure and isolated outliers. These patterns describe how the learned matrices distribute strength across different directions, but their origins and relationship to generalization remain unclear. The paper studies them in a controlled setting: a single-head tied-attention layer trained on synthetic high-dimensional sequence tasks.

Using random matrix theory, spin-glass theory, and approximate message passing, the authors obtain an exact high-dimensional characterization of training and test errors. Their analysis also describes interpolation and recovery thresholds and the spectra of key and query matrices. It predicts the full singular-value distribution of the trained query-key map, including its low-rank structure and isolated spectral outliers.

These predictions qualitatively agree with observations from more realistic transformers, while the exact characterization belongs to the specified synthetic setting. For targets with power-law spectra, the paper shows that learning progressively recovers spectral components, producing power-law scaling laws. This connects the structure being learned to both the resulting weight spectrum and the way predictive performance scales.
icml-2026-single-head-attention-in-high-.tldr: A high-dimensional theory of single-head attention connects learned weight spectra, generalization, and power-law scaling through sequential spectral recovery.

paragraphs: Human judgments are a central standard for evaluating AI, but different annotators can produce different system rankings. Majority voting discards information about annotator reliability and how ambiguous an individual item is. STABLEVAL treats this disagreement as something to model explicitly when estimating system quality and assessing the stability of comparisons.

The framework models latent item correctness together with annotator-specific confusion patterns. It uses those estimates to assign posterior expected credit to items and calibrated scores to systems. Its objective is stable evaluation with uncertainty represented in the scores, rather than recovering a single hard label for each example. Ranking stability is formalized as an evaluation objective in its own right.

Controlled synthetic experiments and multiple human-annotated benchmarks show that majority voting becomes less accurate and less stable under annotator heterogeneity and adversarial noise. STABLEVAL produces more stable, statistically grounded rankings in these evaluations. The findings show why the way judgments are aggregated can materially affect conclusions about AI systems, even when the underlying collection of human evaluations is the starting point.
icml-2026-stableval-disagreement-aware-a.tldr: STABLEVAL models annotator disagreement and item uncertainty to produce more stable AI system scores and rankings.

paragraphs: The paper studies a fundamental imbalance between those who train a model and those who receive it. It constructs backdoors for a broad class of deep feedforward networks that are statistically difficult to distinguish from honest training, even when the recipient can inspect the complete model, including all of its weights.

The indistinguishability statement uses total variation distance: the distributions of backdoored and honestly trained models are close in this statistical sense. Possession of the backdoor enables invariance-based adversarial examples for every input. These examples map inputs that are far apart to outputs that are unusually close, exposing a hidden capability available to the trainer.

Without the backdoor, producing any such adversarial examples in polynomial time is provably impossible under standard cryptographic assumptions. This computational claim is distinct from the statistical claim about identifying the altered model. Together, the theory and preliminary empirical findings show how full model access can coexist with a substantial capability advantage for the adversarial trainer in the construction studied.
icml-2026-statistically-undetectable-bac.tldr: The paper constructs neural-network backdoors that remain statistically hidden under full inspection while giving their holder privileged access to adversarial examples.

paragraphs: This paper frames generative-model unlearning as estimating a density ratio toward a desired target distribution. Classifier guidance can approximate that ratio, but the authors show a finite-sample failure case: it may not faithfully forget data whose distribution is sharply concentrated. The difficulty is tied to that concentration rather than a general impossibility of classifier-guided unlearning.

Temper-Then-Tilt Unlearning keeps the base model frozen and changes inference in two steps. Tempering first flattens high-confidence peaks in the base distribution. Tilting then uses a lightweight classifier trained to distinguish retained samples from forgotten samples to reshape the tempered distribution. The ordering is central because the classifier operates after those peaks have been softened.

The analysis gives finite-sample guarantees connecting classifier risk with unlearning quality and proves the necessity of tempering for concentrated distributions in the studied setting. On TOFU, experiments report improved forgetting and generative utility over existing baselines while training only a fraction of the parameters with minimal runtime. The results connect a specific distributional failure mode to a targeted inference procedure.
icml-2026-temper-then-tilt-principled-un.tldr: T3-Unlearning flattens a frozen model’s concentrated probability peaks before applying classifier guidance, improving forgetting and utility on TOFU.

paragraphs: As context lengths grow, this paper asks how quickly attention over a finite set of tokens approaches its infinite-token limit. It calls that rate token sample complexity. The analysis distinguishes convergence of the attention map itself from convergence of moments describing the distribution of output tokens, giving two views of long-context behavior.

For compactly supported and more generally sub-Gaussian distributions, the attention map converges uniformly over a radius-R ball at rate C(R)/sqrt(n). However, C(R) grows exponentially with R, weakening the estimate for large radii. The moment analysis instead obtains a rate C′(R)/n^β, with β below one-half and a prefactor depending polynomially on support size.

That exponent depends on attention geometry and spectral properties of the token distribution. The authors also establish logarithmic convergence when the attention parameter grows toward the hardmax regime. Synthetic and real-data experiments support the predictions and connect the predicted slowdown to downstream accuracy. These results show that increasing token count can yield convergence whose pace depends strongly on the attention regime and token distribution.
icml-2026-token-sample-complexity-of-att.tldr: Token sample complexity quantifies how attention approaches its infinite-context limit and reveals geometry-dependent slowdowns, especially near hardmax.

paragraphs: A benchmark’s aggregate score can hide two different problems: a model may struggle with a specific concept, or the benchmark may cover that concept poorly. This paper develops an automatic method to expose both kinds of gap. It uses concept activations from sparse autoencoders to break evaluation into finer-grained, concept-level assessments.

Grounding the analysis in internal model representations provides a shared basis for comparing performance and coverage across benchmarks. The authors apply the method to five open-source models and more than a dozen benchmarks as illustrative examples. The procedure is unsupervised, allowing gaps to emerge without requiring a predefined catalog of every potential model weakness.

As validation, it recovers previously documented weaknesses, including ones related to sycophancy, while also identifying new model gaps. It additionally uncovers missing coverage of concepts that belong within benchmark scope. The contribution is a complement to established evaluations: concept-level decomposition helps explain what aggregate scores conceal and gives benchmark developers information they can use when revising coverage.
icml-2026-uncovering-competency-gaps-in-.tldr: Sparse-autoencoder concept activations reveal model weaknesses and benchmark coverage gaps hidden by aggregate evaluation scores.

paragraphs: SHAP explains predictions by assigning contributions to input features, but exact computation for neural networks involves an exponentially growing search space over those features. This makes precise explanations computationally difficult as the space expands. Verified SHAP takes a step toward larger exact computations by drawing on advances in neural network verification.

The proposed algorithm computes guaranteed lower and upper bounds on each SHAP value. These bounds can become arbitrarily tight and ultimately recover the exact values. This provides a way to narrow uncertainty about an explanation while preserving mathematical guarantees about where the true contribution lies throughout the bounding process.

The authors demonstrate search spaces orders of magnitude larger than those handled by state-of-the-art exact methods. They present this as an initial step toward scaling exact SHAP, rather than a general removal of its computational difficulty. The resulting bounds and exact values also provide a principled reference for evaluating statistical approximation methods on larger spaces, helping assess how faithfully approximate explanations reflect the quantities they seek to estimate.
icml-2026-verified-shap-provable-bounds-.tldr: Verified SHAP uses neural network verification to tighten provable attribution bounds and recover exact values on substantially larger search spaces.

paragraphs: Forecasting future scenes through RGB video is computationally costly and requires another step to obtain decision-relevant information. Predicting specific outputs such as segmentation directly requires labels. This paper instead forecasts vision foundation model features, which contain semantic and geometric information that can be decoded without requiring downstream-task labels during forecasting training.

The authors show that regression-based forecasting struggles with partial observations because it averages over plausible futures. Simply replacing regression with generative flow matching still produces worse samples, despite fitting the uncertainty of the task mathematically. Their central insight is that these features need an autoencoded, compact latent representation suitable for diffusion.

The proposed latent space preserves information better than uncompressed feature diffusion and PCA-based compression in the evaluated settings. The benefits extend across forecasting and applications such as image generation. These results suggest that conditional generation of compressed foundation-model features could support scalable scene forecasting while representing alternative futures. The contribution ties the effectiveness of generative forecasting to the representation in which generation takes place.
icml-2026-vfmf-dense-forecasting-by-gene.tldr: VFMF forecasts future scenes by generating foundation-model features in a learned compact latent space that better supports diffusion.
